articles.title: The Federal Reserve Should Raise Interest Rates Today, but It Won't for One Fundamental Reason
articles.description: Hard economic data, not proactive guesswork, drive Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) policy decisions.
articles.content: Today is a pivotal day for Wall Street's major stock indexes, the Dow Jones Industrial Average , S&P 500 , and Nasdaq Composite , as well as consumers. Mere hours from now, the 12 voting members of th... [3234 symbols]
articles.summary: The Federal Reserve (FOMC) is set to make its decision on interest rates on July 29, a pivotal day for Wall Street's major stock indexes. While the probability of the Fed raising the federal funds target rate has tripled from 12.8% to 37.9%, this is unlikely as the FOMC is a reactive, not proactive, body. Energy supply issues such as Iran's disruption of the Strait of Hormuz and rising oil prices have increased costs for businesses and consumers. The early stages of "Trumpflation" are also contributing to inflation, driven by President Donald Trump's policies. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has removed forward-looking guidance from his first FOMM meeting, arguing this could hamstring policymakers' decisions. While it is unlikely the Fed will adjust interest rates later today (July 29), there is an exceptionally high probability of a rate hike at the Sept. 15-16 FOMc meeting. If interest rates do rise, it could hinder the partially debt-financed artificial intelligence data center build-out and halt Wall Street’s parabolic rallies.
articles.shortSummary: The Federal Reserve is unlikely to raise interest rates today due to rising energy prices, but potential rate changes at other meetings will occur.

articles.summary: The Federal Reserve voted to keep its key interest rate steady despite opposition from three regional presidents, Beth Hammack of Cleveland, Neel Kashkari of Minneapolis, and Lorie Logan of Dallas, who had expressed a desire for higher rates. Despite increasing support among some officials for a rate increase, the Federal Open Market Committee voted 9-3 to leave the federal funds rate in a range between 3.5% and 3.75%. The dissenting votes challenged Chairman Kevin Warsh's ability to provide clear road signs on where monetary policy is headed, leading to an unusually high level of uncertainty for the meeting. The post-meeting statement stated that the three dissenters preferred to raise the target range for the federal funding rate by a ¼ percentage point.

articles.title: President Trump Wanted A Rate Cut—The Fed Gave Him A Rate Hike
articles.description: The Federal Reserve unanimously raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter percentage point Wednesday, rebuffing President Donald Trump’s calls for lower borrowing costs.The Federal Open Market Committee lifted the target range for the federal funds rate from 3.5%-3.75% to 3.75%-4.0%. It was the central bank’s first rate increase in more than three years, going against Trump’s calls to lower interest rates.“Lower the interest rates,” Trump said. “Because the U.S.A. is a much stronger credit than it was just a short time ago.” Trump says the United States’ strength should translate into lower borrowing costs. The Fed, however, is confronting inflation that has remained above its 2% objective for more than five years. Year-over-year inflation held steady at 3.4% during the 12 months ending in August, as monthly price growth accelerated on higher energy costs, according to data the Bureau of Labor Statistics released last week. The higher numbers were driven primarily by higher energy costs as oil prices rose amid rising tensions in the Middle East. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh told Congress in July that policymakers would remain focused on bringing inflation under control. “The members of our committee have no tolerance for persistently elevated inflation,” Warsh said. “And we share a resolute commitment to restoring price stability.” Warsh explained recent inflation is hurting the American people. “It has been a tax on the American people and businesses. We plan on getting rid of that tax,” he said. “That means we need a regime change in policy, and we need new consideration of practices, some of which have been working, some of which haven’t.”President Trump has previously blamed other Federal Reserve officials rather than Warsh for policy decisions in which he disagreed.“They have a board and Kevin’s fantastic, but he’s got a board and the board members are very political, I would say,” Trump said when asked about the central bank in July. “I know what he wants to do, but you need the consent of some people that have, perhaps, bad intentions.”Days after Trump’s comments, Warsh praised his colleagues and emphasized unity.“I am truly lucky to work with colleagues so capable and mission-focused and so determined like I am, to sharpen the performance of the Federal Reserve,” he said. “Not one of my FOMC colleagues is under any illusion. We have begun a new chapter and we understand that the 5+ years of inflation above target cannot be cured in 9 weeks or by a single month of modest price decreases.”

articles.summary: The Federal Reserve Open Market Committee (FOCM) is expected to raise interest rates to address inflation caused by the Iran war and a stronger than expected economy. Since September 2024, the Fed has reduced the overnight bank borrowing rate by 1.75 percentage points. The federal funds target range is 1.25 percentage points lower today than it was after the September 2024 meeting, falling from 4.75%–5.00% to 3.50%–3.75%. This reflects skepticism among lenders that inflation could return down to the Fed’s 2%. Meanwhile, 30-year mortgage rates are three percentage points higher than just before the Ukraine war, with the 10-year Treasury rate at 4.58%. Other inflationary pressures include rising fuel prices, decreased wages for low-income households, decreased car purchases, and increased borrowing for gas. The Fed has been unsuccessful in reducing lower-term borrowing costs. The labor market appears to be recovering on its own money, but could cause more rapid adoption of artificial intelligence and investing software.
articles.shortSummary: The Federal Reserve should avoid raising interest rates due to inflation and other factors, particularly the war with Iran and severe weather.

articles.summary: The Federal Reserve has announced that it will raise interest rates for the first time in three years. The Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System approved the decision by a 12-0 vote. The move is seen as a move in support of the Fed's dual mandate and aims to reduce inflation. Financial advisor Nate Kreinbrink, who believes the move may not immediately impact the economy, said borrowers shouldn't panic at the idea of a hike and that the Fed is not likely to be swayed by political pressure. articles.summary: The Federal Reserve (Fed) is expected to raise interest rates in 2026, according to CME's FedWatch. This is good news for investors as rates lower borrowing costs, leading to economic growth and rising stock prices. However, when the Fed raises rates, which increases borrowing costs and increases expenses, can negatively impact companies' investments. The benchmark federal funds rate had been near zero for six years after the Great Recession and never exceeded the 2.25% to 2.50% range in the rate-hiking cycle that followed, peaking in July 2019. Since then, rates have plateaued at the 3.50%. However, expectations have changed, with 51% expecting a rate hike in October and 70% expecting rates to be higher by December.

articles.summary: The Federal Reserve recently delivered one of the most anticipated interest rate decisions in years, leaving its federal funds target rate unchanged at 3.5% to 3.75%. However, this decision was overshadowed by Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's decision to abandon forward-looking guidance from the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting statements. This move has caused concern among Wall Street, as Warsh, who was only the 17th head of the Fed since its inception in December 1913, and four FOMC members, including Warsh and Beth Hammack, Neel Kashkari, and Lorie Logan, disented in favor of a quarter-point rate hike. This is the first time three dissents have occurred in the same policy direction since September 2016. The resulting division and uncertainty could pose a serious problem for the stock market.
articles.shortSummary: The Federal Reserve's latest interest rate decision was marred by multiple dissents, raising concerns about the institution's credibility and forward-looking guidance.

articles.summary: The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) recently saw the first time in 56 years that three FOMC members had dissenting so early in the tenure of a new Fed chair. While the Federal Reserve held interest rates steady at 3.5%-3.75%, three members favored a quarter-point rate hike. This decision sparked a surge in the Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite. While there is a real possibility that the Fed will raise interest rates to stabilize prices, there are two nontraditional methods that can increase interest rates without adjusting the federal funds target rate. The removal of forward-looking guidance from FOMCs meeting statements has also been seen as having a significant impact on interest rates. Additionally, the Fed can influence interest rates through deleveraging the Fed's balance sheet, which grew tenfold between August 2008 and March 2022 to nearly $9 trillion.
